subjects/physics/intermediate/waves-and-: Ever wonder why a violin and a truck horn sound so different? Stretch a live wave on screen, tweak its height and speed, and hear how those tweaks change loudness and pitch.
subjects/chemistry/intermediate/chemical: Think of electrons as the glue holding every material together. This lesson shows the three gluing styles — swapping, sharing and pooling electrons — and teaches you how to tell them apart.
subjects/math/intermediate/the-derivativ: You already know the slope of a straight line. Now slide a point along a curve and watch its steepness change from instant to instant — that's the derivative, and x² turns into 2x.
subjects/history/intermediate/age-of-rev: Once, most people were subjects, not citizens — with almost no say in how they were governed. Follow three centuries of revolutions that toppled kings and built the world of voters and nations we live in.
subjects/political-science/intermediate/: Who decides what a government is allowed to do? See how countries split power into pieces so no leader becomes all-powerful, and why your rights come first — even before the government itself.
subjects/psychology/intermediate/researc: How do psychologists know their discoveries are real and not just luck? Learn the honest-trade tools — testing ideas fairly, controlling experiments, hiding who's in which group, and repeating studies to double-check.
subjects/philosophy/intermediate/politic: Do you really have to obey the government? Weigh four famous thinkers' answers step by careful step, each arguing a different 'deal' between rulers and the ruled — then pick a side.
subjects/math/intermediate/trigonometry: Watch a triangle bend into a wave, then a wave wrap around a circle — and trigonometry suddenly clicks. It's the same sine that draws circles, carries sound and swings pendulums.
subjects/math/intermediate/sequences-and: Some number patterns climb in even steps; others double like folding paper. Meet both families, then learn the famous trick that adds up a long list in seconds instead of hours.
subjects/math/intermediate/exponentials-: Doubling is sneaky: start with one coin and after 30 doublings you'd be a billionaire. See how powers make things explode or fade, and how logarithms act as the undo button for exponents.
subjects/math/intermediate/counting-and-: How many ways can you arrange ten books on a shelf? More than three million. Learn to count without listing everything — arrangements, groups, and the pigeonhole rule that forces two things to share.
subjects/math/intermediate/circles-and-c: Algebra meets the compass here. Plot points, slide shapes, and discover that a circle is just an equation in disguise — one you can pin anywhere on the grid.
subjects/physics/intermediate/projectile: When you throw a ball, two things happen at once: it sails sideways and falls downward, completely independently. This lesson splits those motions apart and explains why every throw traces the same kind of arc.
subjects/physics/intermediate/momentum-a: Crash two carts together and check the books — momentum never disappears. See why heavier, faster things are harder to stop, and how this one rule explains every collision from marbles to car wrecks.
subjects/physics/intermediate/circular-m: Here's a mind-bender: the Moon is constantly falling — it just keeps missing Earth. Discover how sideways speed plus gravity creates orbits, and why astronauts float with no engine running.
subjects/physics/intermediate/thermal-ph: Heat always sneaks from hot to cold, and no machine can cheat that. Meet the laws of the universe nothing can dodge, and find out what temperature really measures inside stuff.
subjects/physics/intermediate/electrosta: Rub a balloon on your hair and it clings to the wall. Zoom in to see why: tiny charges pushing and pulling across empty space, following one simple rule that weakens fast with distance.
subjects/physics/intermediate/circuits-a: Electricity keeps tidy books. Build circuits, push voltage around like water pressure, and learn the accounting rules that make every current and every bulb's brightness in a circuit add up exactly.
subjects/physics/intermediate/magnetism-: Spin a magnet near a coil of wire and electricity appears — that's how almost every power station works. Watch moving charges create magnets and moving magnets create currents, round and round.
subjects/physics/intermediate/optics-len: Trace light rays as they bend through lenses and bounce off mirrors, and you'll finally see why glasses fix blurry vision and telescopes gather starlight. Draw every ray yourself.
subjects/chemistry/intermediate/chemical: Some reactions run both directions at once, like a tug-of-war that settles into a tie. Nudge one side and watch the whole balance shift — chemists use this trick to squeeze out more product.
subjects/chemistry/intermediate/thermody: Why do some reactions give off heat while others soak it up? Measure the energy flowing in and out of reactions, and solve the puzzle of why some 'impossible' ones happen anyway.
subjects/chemistry/intermediate/reaction: What makes one reaction finish in a flash and another take years? Test the speed controls — temperature, concentration and catalysts — and find the energy hill molecules must climb before they can react.
subjects/chemistry/intermediate/redox-an: Batteries, rust and fireworks all come down to electrons hopping between chemicals. Follow those hops to see why metal corrodes, how batteries push current, and how to slow or speed the whole process.
subjects/chemistry/intermediate/organic-: Carbon is the Lego brick of chemistry: it snaps into chains and rings that make up petrol, plastics and perfumes. Build the family tree of carbon compounds, from simple links to sweet-smelling rings.
subjects/biology/intermediate/enzymes-an: Inside every cell, tiny protein machines grab molecules and speed up reactions enormously. Meet these helpers, follow the assembly lines they form, and see how your body runs thousands of reactions at once.
subjects/biology/intermediate/genetics-i: Why can two brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child? Fill in Punnett squares to predict which traits appear, then read family trees like a detective to uncover inheritance's hidden rules.
subjects/biology/intermediate/the-immune: Your body keeps a memory of every germ it has ever beaten. See how fast, general defenders hold the line while slow, precise ones learn the enemy — and how vaccines give them a practice run.
subjects/biology/intermediate/plant-biol: Plants drink through their roots, pump water up tubes thinner than hairs, and whisper to themselves with chemical signals. Explore the hidden plumbing and hormones that turn a seed into a giant tree.
subjects/biology/intermediate/neurobiolo: Your nerves are living wires carrying sparks of charged atoms. Follow a signal racing from your hand to your spinal cord — the reflex shortcut that makes you yank back before you've even thought about it.
subjects/biology/intermediate/gas-exchan: Take a deep breath and follow the oxygen: it slips through balloon-thin air sacs into your blood, then swaps places with carbon dioxide. A breathing lab shows the pressures that keep everything moving.
subjects/biology/intermediate/excretion-: Your kidneys clean your blood dozens of times every day without you noticing. Follow a single drop of blood through their tiny filters to see what gets kept, what gets dumped, and how urine forms.
subjects/biology/intermediate/reproducti: Growing a new human is a months-long project run by chemical messengers. Watch how hormones switch stages on and off, and spot the feedback loops — the same trick a thermostat uses — steering the whole cycle.
subjects/astronomy/intermediate/telescop: Visible light is only one flavor of the universe's messages. Tour telescopes that see radio whispers, heat and X-rays, and find out why some of them must orbit in space to work at all.
subjects/astronomy/intermediate/the-moon: Why does the Moon change shape night after night, and how can midday suddenly turn dark? Play with the geometry of shadows to master phases, eclipses and even the tides at your local beach.
subjects/astronomy/intermediate/stellar-: Stars are born in dusty clouds and die in gigantic explosions — and the iron in your blood was forged inside one. Follow a star's whole life, from glowing cradle to supernova.
subjects/astronomy/intermediate/the-milk: You live inside a galaxy so vast that light needs 100,000 years to cross it. Spin the map to see our spiral's glowing arms, and visit the monster black hole at the center.
subjects/earth-science/intermediate/volc: Not every volcano explodes — some ooze like thick soup, others blast like shaken soda. Compare runny and sticky magmas to predict each eruption style, and watch melted rock harden into brand-new stone.
subjects/earth-science/intermediate/eart: When rocks snap deep underground, the shockwave races around the whole planet. Learn to read a seismograph's squiggles, pinpoint where a quake started, and understand how scientists measure its size.
subjects/earth-science/intermediate/atmo: Weather is just air on the move, pushed around by invisible pressure differences. Follow a storm from flat gray skies to the moment the rain finally falls — and see why it fell at all.
subjects/earth-science/intermediate/ocea: The ocean hides a giant conveyor belt that slowly drags water around the entire planet, warming some lands and cooling others. Trace its loops and see why a current shift can change weather everywhere.
subjects/environmental-science/intermedi: Every species that disappears is a book burned before anyone read it. Map where life is richest, measure what's vanishing, and test which conservation efforts actually bring endangered places back.

The water under your feet hides in sponge-like rock layers that can take centuries to refill. Follow water from underground store to your tap, see how pollution sneaks in, and how treatment plants clean it back up.
You can't see the tiniest air pollution, yet those specks slip deep into your lungs. Learn what's floating around you, which particles hurt people most, and why air quality is measured like medicine.

Flip a light switch and hundreds of power plants adjust within seconds. Follow electricity from generator to socket, and watch the balancing act of adding wind and solar to a grid built around steady fuels.

There's no such place as 'away' — everything you throw out goes somewhere. Compare recycling's promises with its real costs, and explore smarter designs where today's rubbish becomes tomorrow's raw material.
subjects/agriculture/intermediate/soil-h: A handful of healthy soil holds more living things than there are people on Earth. Dig into what makes soil good at growing food — its crumbly structure, its microscopic workforce, its stash of carbon.
subjects/agriculture/intermediate/plant-: Plants eat too, and their favorite menu items are labeled N, P and K. Find out what those letters feed, why timing matters, and how leftover fertilizer washes into rivers and causes trouble downstream.
subjects/agriculture/intermediate/pests-: Battling pests with spray alone is an arms race you eventually lose. See how farmers stack clever tricks — pest-eating insects, crop rotation, careful timing — so chemicals become the last resort instead of the first move.
subjects/agriculture/intermediate/animal: Raising animals for food is part biology, part bookkeeping, and part ethics. Compare feeding systems, check what good welfare looks like on a farm, and follow how feed turns into milk, eggs and meat.
subjects/agriculture/intermediate/farm-e: A farm can grow beautiful crops and still go broke. Work through the numbers — costs, prices, subsidies — and see why world markets and harvest sizes decide which farms survive the year.
subjects/medicine/intermediate/how-docto: Doctors solve mysteries for a living, one clue at a time. Try their method yourself: list the possible causes, weigh the evidence, and dodge the mental trap of falling for your very first guess.
subjects/medicine/intermediate/pharmacol: Why does one pill cure a headache while too many of another can poison you? Follow a medicine through your body — where it binds, how long it lasts, and how different drugs can clash.
subjects/medicine/intermediate/infection: Antibiotics were a miracle — and germs have been fighting back ever since. Learn what separates bacteria from viruses, why antibiotics can't cure a cold, and how resistance turns treatable diseases scary again.
subjects/medicine/intermediate/public-he: When a disease breaks out, special detectives get to work counting cases and tracing spread. Meet epidemiology, the science of sick populations, and see how one number predicts whether an outbreak explodes or fizzles.
subjects/neuroscience/intermediate/brain: Your brain has neighborhoods, each with its own specialty — one for vision, one for language, one for planning your next move. Take the tour and meet the regions that add up to you.
subjects/neuroscience/intermediate/neuro: Brain cells never quite touch — a gap far thinner than a hair separates them. Watch chemical messengers leap across that gap, and see how every thought depends on millions of these tiny crossings.
subjects/neuroscience/intermediate/the-a: Neurons talk in electric spikes that switch on and off within a thousandth of a second. Replay the famous experiments that decoded the spike, and see why the message never fades along the wire.
subjects/neuroscience/intermediate/sense: Everything you've ever seen, heard or felt is your brain's translation of raw signals. Follow light from your eyeball to your cortex and watch sensation become the colorful world you live in.
subjects/neuroscience/intermediate/movem: Catching a ball takes three brain areas working like a team: one plans the move, one smooths it, one picks the habit. See how their teamwork turns a thought into a swing of your arm.
subjects/psychology/intermediate/percept: Illusions aren't just party tricks — they're x-ray windows into your brain's shortcuts. Use famous illusions to catch your visual system's rules in action, even when those rules get the answer hilariously wrong.
subjects/psychology/intermediate/develop: Babies truly believe that a toy you hide behind your back stops existing. Follow how thinking transforms from infancy to adulthood, and how today's scientists tested, tweaked and sometimes overturned the classic stages.
subjects/psychology/intermediate/social-: Why do kind people follow the crowd, and what makes an advert convincing? Explore the invisible forces between people — how we explain each other's behavior, form attitudes, and get nudged into changing our minds.
subjects/psychology/intermediate/persona: Are you the way you are because of genes, upbringing, or choices? Explore how psychologists measure personality with the famous Big Five traits, and what those test results can — and can't — tell you.
subjects/psychology/intermediate/abnorma: How do therapists decide what actually helps? Step inside treatments like CBT, see which methods pass rigorous scientific tests, and find out why diagnosing a mind is so much trickier than diagnosing a bone.
subjects/sociology/intermediate/class-an: Where your family starts often shapes where you finish — but not always. Examine the ladder of wealth and opportunity, measure who climbs it, and see how advantage quietly passes down the generations.
subjects/sociology/intermediate/race-eth: The boxes people get sorted into feel natural, but history built them. Investigate where categories like race and ethnicity came from, what they still shape today, and how identity works from the inside.
subjects/sociology/intermediate/gender-a: Ideas about what 'boys do' and 'girls do' have changed massively in one century. Look at the roles we're handed, the norms we absorb, and the evidence on how those roles really shift.
subjects/sociology/intermediate/deviance: Why do people break rules, and what actually makes them stop? Test tough-on-crime ideas against the evidence, and see how labeling someone 'a criminal' can push them deeper into crime.
subjects/anthropology/intermediate/the-f: Anthropology studies humans from four angles at once: their cultures, their bones, their languages and the objects they left behind. Peek into each toolkit and see how the four combine into one big picture.
subjects/anthropology/intermediate/human: Meet your ancient relatives — from Lucy, who climbed trees over three million years ago, to Neanderthals who made tools and cared for their sick. Walk the timeline from ape-like ancestors to modern humans.
subjects/anthropology/intermediate/kinsh: Who counts as family? Cultures answer that question in wildly different ways — some trace relatives through mothers, some through fathers, some through both. Compare the rules and see how societies organize inheritance, loyalty and belonging.
subjects/anthropology/intermediate/archa: Archaeologists read trash like history books. Dig layer by layer into their methods, and see how broken pots and buried coins get pinned to surprisingly exact dates using clever science.
subjects/political-science/intermediate/: Liberalism, conservatism and socialism aren't just internet insults — they're serious, century-old arguments about how society should be run. Hear each side's best case and work out where you'd land.
The way votes get counted can change who wins the very same election. Compare voting systems side by side, watch each produce a different result, and judge which flaws you could live with.
Why do countries sometimes behave like rivals on a playground with no teacher? Try on three big theories of world politics and use each to predict what nations will do next.
Turning a good idea into a working law is a long relay race with plenty of dropped batons. Follow one policy from first spark to final report card, with real cases along the way.
subjects/law/intermediate/sources-of-law: When two rules disagree, which one wins? Climb law's ladder — constitution on top, everyday regulations below — and see how judges use past cases as stepping stones to decide new ones.
subjects/law/intermediate/criminal-vs-ci: One person can be found not guilty of a crime yet still owe millions in a civil case. Unpack the two systems' different goals, different burdens of proof, and different powers over your life.
subjects/law/intermediate/how-a-case-mov: A lawsuit travels a long road: complaint, answer, evidence, trial, maybe appeal. Walk it step by step and see what actually happens at each stop — no TV drama required.
subjects/finance/intermediate/budgeting-: Money problems are usually math problems in disguise. Build a simple budget, learn why an emergency stash matters more than you'd think, and find the smartest order for paying off debts.
subjects/finance/intermediate/stocks-and: Buying a stock makes you a tiny part-owner of a company; buying a bond makes you the company's lender. See how each one pays you back, and why their risks are opposites.
subjects/finance/intermediate/diversific: Don't put all your eggs in one basket — but why does mixing actually work? Run a portfolio experiment and watch wobbly investments combine into something steadier than any single one alone.
subjects/finance/intermediate/financial-: Companies keep three diaries: what they own and owe, what they earned, and where their cash went. Learn to read all three together and spot both healthy businesses and hidden problems.
subjects/finance/intermediate/time-value: Would you rather have $100 today or $100 next year? Today, obviously — and there's real math behind that gut feeling. Learn to compare money across time and judge future promises honestly.
subjects/business/intermediate/what-a-bu: Every business does two things: create something people value, and try to keep part of that value for itself. Sort real companies into winners and strugglers using this simple two-part lens.
subjects/business/intermediate/customers: You can't sell to 'everyone' — and businesses that try usually sell to nobody. Learn how companies pick their exact crowd, position their product to fit it, and know when a product truly matches a market.
subjects/business/intermediate/marketing: Marketing is much more than ads: it's the four Ps — product, price, place, promotion — working as a team. Trace a customer's journey from first glance to loyal fan, and see where the money goes.
subjects/business/intermediate/operation: A small delay at one factory can empty shelves on another continent. Follow products along supply chains, play with inventory levels, and see why small orders balloon as they travel upstream.
subjects/business/intermediate/people-an: Great companies aren't just clever ideas — they're people pulling in the same direction. Explore how hiring, rewards and culture shape a team, and why honest incentives beat clever ones.
subjects/philosophy/intermediate/philoso: Is your mind just your brain, or something more? Wrestle with philosophy's hardest puzzle — why does thinking feel like anything at all — and ask whether a robot could ever truly feel too.

How can science be so trustworthy if every theory might someday be proven wrong? Meet the philosophers who built science's rulebook and follow their great arguments about what separates real science from clever guesswork.
subjects/philosophy/intermediate/eastern: Western philosophy has famous names, but India, China and Japan built deep traditions of their own. Explore ideas from the Upanishads to Zen, including ancient questions about the self that still feel brand new.
subjects/philosophy/intermediate/aesthet: Why does one painting move you while another leaves you cold? Take on the oldest question about art — what is beauty? — and practice defending your taste with reasons instead of shrugs.
subjects/religious-studies/intermediate/: Studying religion academically isn't about deciding which faith is true — it's about comparing them fairly, from both inside and outside. Learn the historian's and anthropologist's tools for taking every tradition seriously.
Hinduism is less one religion than a vast, ancient family of traditions going back some 3,000 years. Travel from the earliest hymns to today's devotional songs and see how the many paths connect.
A prince walked away from his palace to figure out why life involves suffering — and his answer grew into one of the world's great traditions. Follow Buddhism's core ideas as it spread across Asia.
Judaism is a 3,000-year conversation between a people, their law and their sacred texts. Follow the covenant story from ancient times to today, and see how studying itself became a sacred act.
How did a small group following a teacher from Nazareth become the world's largest religion? Trace the story — the great splits, the art and arguments, and the spread across every continent.

Islam began with one man's message in seventh-century Arabia and soon stretched across continents. Learn the five pillars, meet the Sunni–Shia divide, and explore the golden age when Muslim scholars led the world in science.
subjects/literature/intermediate/close-r: Great writers hide whole worlds inside single word choices. Learn to slow down and interrogate a sentence — why that word, that image, that rhythm — and build an argument that proves what you noticed.
subjects/literature/intermediate/poetry-: Poetry has a heartbeat you can tap out with your hand. Learn to scan — marking stressed and unstressed beats — and hear how rhythm carries meaning, from strict sonnets to free verse.
subjects/literature/intermediate/figures: 'Time is a thief' isn't literally true, and that's exactly the point. Collect the writer's toolbox of comparisons and twists — from simple metaphors to show-off tricks — and learn what each one is for.
subjects/literature/intermediate/the-nov: Four centuries ago the novel as we know it was brand new. Trace the journey from those first great adventure stories to books that dive straight inside a character's head, mid-thought.
subjects/literature/intermediate/shakesp: Shakespeare wrote his plays in verse so packed that actors still puzzle over it today. Uncover his tricks — hidden puns, switched words, disguises — and find out why his lines work best spoken aloud.
subjects/literature/intermediate/world-e: Long before novels, whole cultures told giant stories in verse: heroes, journeys, gods and wars. Sample the world's oldest great tales — Gilgamesh to the Mahabharata — and spot what they all share.
subjects/linguistics/intermediate/phonet: There are sounds in the world's languages you've never noticed your own mouth can make. Learn the alphabet that writes down every human sound, then practice making strange new noises on purpose.
subjects/linguistics/intermediate/phonol: Say 'cat' and 'cap' out loud — the vowels shift slightly, and you never noticed. Discover the hidden rules running beneath every accent, and why some sound swaps feel natural while others sound foreign.
subjects/linguistics/intermediate/morpho: 'Unbelievableness' isn't in any dictionary, yet you understood it instantly — because words are built from parts that snap together. Learn the building rules and how languages assemble words in different ways.
subjects/linguistics/intermediate/syntax: Every sentence you speak is built by rules you never studied on purpose. Draw the hidden tree inside a sentence and see how languages bend the same pieces into different meanings.
subjects/linguistics/intermediate/semant: 'Can you pass the salt?' isn't really a question about your arm muscles. Dive into the gap between what words literally say and what speakers actually mean — and how listeners bridge it instantly.
subjects/languages/intermediate/your-fir: Here's a language-learning cheat code: the most common 1,000 words cover most of everyday conversation. Start with those high-value words and watch your understanding grow like money collecting interest.
subjects/languages/intermediate/pronunci: Your ears were trained by your first language, which is why foreign sounds slip right past you. Use phonetic anchors — familiar landmarks for your mouth — to nail sounds that once seemed impossible.
subjects/languages/intermediate/listenin: The best listening practice isn't grinding through hard audio — it's hearing things just slightly above your level. See how to find that sweet spot and let your brain absorb a language naturally.
subjects/languages/intermediate/grammar-: Forget memorizing grammar tables — your brain learns patterns, not paradigms. Collect real phrases, spot the patterns hiding inside them, and watch grammar fall into place almost on its own.
subjects/languages/intermediate/speaking: Shadowing means speaking along with a native speaker like an echo, a beat behind. It feels silly and works brilliantly — see how it wires pronunciation and rhythm straight into your mouth.
subjects/computer-science/intermediate/a: How does your phone find one contact among thousands in an instant? Race different search and sort strategies side by side, step through every move, and see why some methods crush others as lists grow.
subjects/computer-science/intermediate/p: Code is just instructions a computer follows exactly — doing what you say, not what you mean. Write your first variables, loops and functions in Python and watch them run for real.
subjects/computer-science/intermediate/l: Your computer's brilliance is built from switches that only know on and off. Snap simple gates together into adders and memory, and watch pure logic become a machine that calculates.
subjects/computer-science/intermediate/d: Data can outlive the programs that made it — if you store it well. Compare simple tables with flexible JSON, and learn to write data files that still make sense ten years from now.
subjects/data-science/intermediate/clean: Real data is a mess: missing birthdays, impossible ages, one person's name spelled five different ways. Learn to catch the silent errors that ruin analyses and fix them before they fool anyone.
subjects/data-science/intermediate/explo: Before any fancy model, good analysts simply look. Plot the data every which way, hunt for patterns and oddballs, and let the charts ask questions before the math tries to answer them.
subjects/data-science/intermediate/sql-f: Databases hold mountains of answers, and SQL is the pickaxe. Ask real questions across linked tables — who bought what, when, how often — and watch the database do all the digging.
subjects/data-science/intermediate/chart: A chart can lie without a single false word — just chop the axis and a tiny change looks like a cliff. Learn to build honest charts and to catch the sneaky ones.
subjects/artificial-intelligence/interme: Machines can learn from examples instead of instructions — that's machine learning. Sort out its three flavors: learning from labeled examples, finding hidden groups on their own, and improving through trial, error and rewards.
Inside every AI hums a swarm of tiny number-crunchers, each simpler than a calculator. Build one by hand, layer by layer, and watch it learn — including the famous trick that trains whole networks.
Is this email spam or not? How hot will tomorrow be? Those are the two questions machines answer most — sorting into groups and predicting numbers — and there's an honest way to grade both.
How can a computer tell a cat from a croissant? Peek inside networks that scan images in small patches, layer by layer, until simple edges add up into full recognition.
subjects/materials-science/intermediate/: Diamond and pencil graphite are both pure carbon — so why does one cut glass and the other crumble? Zoom from single atoms to crystal patterns and watch invisible structure become visible strength.

Why do planes use aluminum, pots use ceramic, and helmets use squishy foam? Compare the four great material families — metals, ceramics, polymers and composites — and their trade-offs between strong, hard, light and cheap.
subjects/engineering/intermediate/units-: Engineers answer huge questions with tiny scribbles: how many piano tuners work in a city? How much does a cloud weigh? Learn to estimate anything roughly — and catch impossible designs before they're built.
subjects/engineering/intermediate/forces: Every bridge you cross is a carefully choreographed wrestling match with gravity. Load a beam and watch where stress pools, then discover why triangles beat brute strength.
subjects/engineering/intermediate/thermo: Your car engine, your fridge and a power station all obey the same heat rules. Follow the loops that turn fuel into motion and heat into work, and see why perfect efficiency is forbidden.
subjects/engineering/intermediate/fluid-: Water and air push back when things move through them. Trace fluid flowing through pipes and pumps, watch pressure drop along the way, and find out why plumbing is trickier than it looks.
subjects/architecture/intermediate/what-: A building must stand up, keep you dry, and — ideally — be beautiful, a balancing act architects have argued over for 2,000 years. Test each demand and see how real designs juggle all three.
subjects/architecture/intermediate/plans: Architects speak in drawings: a plan looks down from above, a section slices the building open, and scale shrinks reality onto paper. Learn to read all three — and to draw a room to size.
subjects/architecture/intermediate/a-his: Buildings are history you can touch. Walk from the carved stone columns of ancient temples to raw concrete of the modern age, and learn to date a building just by looking at its bones.
subjects/visual-arts/intermediate/line-s: Every drawing, however complex, is built from line, shape and shading. Practice each element deliberately and discover that skill comes from patient training, not magic talent.
subjects/visual-arts/intermediate/colour: Colors play tricks on each other: the same gray looks warmer next to red than next to blue. Experiment with the color wheel, build harmonious palettes, and see how your eyes decide what you see.
subjects/visual-arts/intermediate/perspe: Artists once struggled to paint a road shrinking into the distance — until they invented a mathematical trick for it. Learn the vanishing-point method that turns flat paper into deep, believable space.
subjects/visual-arts/intermediate/drawin: Here's the twist nobody expects: learning to draw is really learning to see. Train your eyes to catch angles, edges and proportions, and watch your drawings improve even before your hands feel skilled.
subjects/art-history/intermediate/renais: Painters suddenly mastered perspective, wealthy patrons threw money around, and art got dramatic — literally. Compare the Renaissance's calm perfection with the Baroque's theatrical sparkle, and spot what each era was trying to say.
subjects/art-history/intermediate/impres: Squeezable paint tubes freed artists to work outdoors — and painting never fully went back inside. Follow the leap from capturing flickering light to flinging raw emotion straight onto the canvas.
subjects/art-history/intermediate/art-be: The art story doesn't begin and end in Europe. Explore the dazzling traditions of the Islamic world, India, China and Africa — glowing miniatures, monumental bronzes — each with its own logic and genius.
subjects/film/intermediate/shot-sizes-an: Filmmakers speak in shot sizes like a grammar: a wide shot sets the scene, a close-up lets you read a face, an insert whispers a detail. Watch each choice change what a scene means.
subjects/film/intermediate/editing-the-c: Two unrelated shots placed side by side create a story neither tells alone — that's editing's secret power. See how cuts build meaning and rhythm, and how they can quietly lie about time.
subjects/film/intermediate/cinematograph: The same actor can look heroic or villainous depending on where the lights sit. Learn the classic three-light setup, and how shadows, camera angles and color quietly set a film's whole mood.
subjects/film/intermediate/sound-design-: Close your eyes during a scary film and the music alone can frighten you — sound does half the work. Explore how effects and scores steer your emotions without you ever noticing.
subjects/design/intermediate/typography-: Letters have voices: a wedding invitation and a heavy-metal poster don't share fonts for good reason. Learn the craft of type — spacing, weight, style — and hear what your text is really saying.
subjects/design/intermediate/grids-and-l: Magazine pages, apps and websites all secretly sit on invisible grids. Learn how these hidden skeletons turn chaos into order — and when breaking the grid on purpose makes a design pop.
subjects/design/intermediate/ux-research: Designers have strong opinions; users have the real answers. Learn to run interviews, watch real people struggle with a design, and let evidence — not taste — settle the arguments.
subjects/design/intermediate/prototyping: Before writing a single line of code, smart designers scribble. See how cheap sketches and paper prototypes answer big questions early — when a mistake costs a minute instead of a month.
subjects/design/intermediate/accessibili: Good design works for people who can't see well, hear well, or use a mouse at all. Check contrast, structure and labels — and discover that designing for everyone makes things better for anyone.
subjects/journalism/intermediate/news-vs: Not everything in print is news. Learn to tell reporting (what happened) from opinion (what to think about it) from analysis (why it happened) — a skill that makes you much harder to fool.
subjects/journalism/intermediate/the-inv: News stories spill their biggest fact in the very first sentence, then trickle down through the details. See why writers stack stories like upside-down pyramids — so busy readers can quit anytime and still know what matters.
subjects/journalism/intermediate/intervi: A great interview is a conversation with a plan. Practice open questions, brave the awkward silences, and master the follow-up that turns a rehearsed answer into a real story.
subjects/sports-science/intermediate/mus: Your muscles run on three different fuel systems: one for a ten-second sprint, one for a few hard minutes, one for the long haul. Race through each and find out where the energy actually comes from.
subjects/sports-science/intermediate/the: Why do athletes breathe hard even when their legs feel fine? Because your heart and lungs set the delivery limit for oxygen — and training raises that famous ceiling called VO₂max.
subjects/sports-science/intermediate/str: Lifting weights doesn't build muscle directly — it sends a 'grow stronger' signal that your body answers later. Learn how load and volume tune that signal, and why rest days count as part of the workout.
subjects/sports-science/intermediate/nut: Eating for sport isn't just eating more — it's timing. Find out what to eat before, during and after training, how hydration changes everything, and which advice is science and which is just marketing.
subjects/statistics/intermediate/samplin: Pollsters interview 1,000 people and claim to know what 300 million think — and sometimes they're right. Discover when that magic works, and the sneaky sampling mistakes that make polls embarrassingly wrong.
subjects/statistics/intermediate/confide: 'About 52%, give or take 3%' — that 'give or take' is the honest part of any estimate. Learn where error bars come from and the two dials that make them smaller.
subjects/statistics/intermediate/hypothe: Statistics puts ideas on trial: your evidence must beat a skeptical jury. Learn how p-values act as judges, and why two different kinds of mistakes can send the verdict the wrong way.
subjects/statistics/intermediate/correla: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together — and neither causes the other. Learn to draw best-fit lines through scattered data, measure how tightly things track, and remember why correlation never proves cause.
subjects/economics/intermediate/elastici: Raise prices by 10% and do you make more money or lose customers? It depends how sharply shoppers flinch. Play with the sensitivity dial that measures how demand and supply react to price.
subjects/economics/intermediate/market-f: Sometimes free markets make a mess they never have to clean up — think factory smoke drifting over a town. Meet the market's known blind spots and the clever fixes, from taxes to rules, that patch them.
subjects/economics/intermediate/gdp-nati: How do you squeeze an entire country's economy into one number? Follow the counting of everything produced and sold, then see what GDP deliberately leaves out — like unpaid housework and clean air.
subjects/economics/intermediate/unemploy: Why can't everyone who wants a job have one? Explore how wages, hiring and job-hunting push against each other, and why even a healthy economy keeps a little unemployment around on purpose.
subjects/economics/intermediate/fiscal-p: When a government spends more than it collects in taxes, where does the gap come from? Follow national budgets through booms and slumps, and see when borrowing is reckless and when it's smart.
subjects/economics/intermediate/monetary: One quiet committee meeting can change the price of everything from mortgages to bread. Learn how central banks steer whole economies using a single dial — the interest rate — and why they turn it slowly.
subjects/history/intermediate/ancient-gr: The ideas you live with — voting, courts, citizenship — were stress-tested in ancient Athens and Rome. Go deeper than the myths and see how those long-ago experiments still echo in today's world.
subjects/history/intermediate/the-islami: While much of Europe dozed, Baghdad blazed with new ideas: algebra, hospitals, star charts and philosophy. Tour the golden age when scholars from Baghdad to Córdoba pushed science forward by leaps.
subjects/history/intermediate/colonialis: A few small countries once ruled most of the planet — and the effects still shape today's maps, borders and bank accounts. Examine how empires were built, what they took, and what they left behind.
subjects/history/intermediate/the-histor: Science wasn't always labs and journals — it began as curious people arguing about nature. Trace how guessing became experimenting became modern research, one breakthrough and one blunder at a time.
subjects/history/intermediate/revolution: In one wild spring, people across Europe rose up demanding rights, freedom and nations of their own — and almost all the uprisings failed. Find out why they erupted, and why their ideas outlived their defeats.
subjects/history/intermediate/unificatio: Italy and Germany were jigsaw puzzles of little states until masterminds stitched them into single nations by 1871. Meet the dreamers, schemers and iron-willed politicians who did the stitching — and what it cost.
subjects/history/intermediate/the-americ: America once split in two and fought itself over slavery, at the cost of hundreds of thousands of lives. Follow the conflict that decided what kind of nation the United States would become.
subjects/history/intermediate/the-treaty: After World War I, three leaders sat down to build a peace — and their deal helped set the stage for World War II. See what each wanted, what they got, and the price paid.
subjects/history/intermediate/the-league: Then came a bold experiment: a club of nations sworn to stop wars together. Explore the League's real successes in the 1920s — and the fatal weaknesses that let the next war sneak through.
subjects/geography/intermediate/maps-pro: You can't flatten an orange peel without tearing it — and the same goes for mapping the round Earth. Learn why every flat map lies somewhere, how to pick your lies, and how digital maps stack data on top.
subjects/geography/intermediate/rivers-f: Rivers are planet-shapers: they carve valleys, carry soil, build deltas — and occasionally flood your street. Follow a river from hilltop spring to the sea, and see why ancient civilizations always settled on its banks.
subjects/geography/intermediate/coasts-a: Beaches aren't permanent — they're sand in constant motion, pushed by every wave and tide. Watch coastlines rebuild themselves day after day, and see how the sea keeps redrawing the edge of the land.
subjects/geography/intermediate/urban-ge: Why is your city exactly where it is — and not fifty miles away? Uncover the forces that plant cities near harbors and crossroads, then watch them sprawl, stack and specialize as they grow.
subjects/geography/intermediate/monsoons: For billions of people, the year isn't split into summer and winter — it's split into wet and dry. See the giant seasonal wind machine that delivers the rains whole villages build their lives around.
subjects/geography/intermediate/climate-: Carbon dioxide is tiny in the air but mighty in its effects. Trace the rising carbon curve, sort natural causes from human ones, and follow the ripple effects from a single farm to the whole globe.
subjects/geography/intermediate/developm: Where you're born predicts a shocking amount about how your life will go. Plot countries on maps of wealth, health and education, and see the world's uneven scoreboard — plus the places beating the odds.
subjects/music/intermediate/rhythm-and-t: Music is math you can dance to. Tap out beats, count the patterns that make songs march or swing, and discover syncopation — the art of landing on the beats nobody expects.
subjects/music/intermediate/scales-and-k: Why do just 12 notes rule all of music? Climb a scale, hear how a key sets a song's home base and shapes its journey, and find out why songs can start on any note.
subjects/music/intermediate/harmony-and-: Play three notes at once and you've built a chord — plus a feeling. Stack chords into progressions and hear the push-pull of tension and release that makes songs want to come home.
subjects/music/intermediate/instruments-: A violin and a flute can play the exact same note and sound nothing alike. Zoom into the sound waves and spot the overtone fingerprint that gives every instrument its own voice.
subjects/music/intermediate/reading-nota: Musicians share a code that's been evolving for 900 years: sheet music. Decode the staff, the notes and the symbols, and read a melody straight off the page like text.
